source: The frameworks of $100M Leads (Alex Hormozi, 2023), restated in this app's own words and turned into exercises. The book is the reference; nothing here quotes it. Chapter numbers point the reader back to it.
confidenceNote: Frameworks and exercises, not figures. The one rule of thumb carried as a number is the book's: lifetime gross profit should be at least three times what a customer cost to get, and the first thirty days should pay back twice that cost before you scale ads.

bands.name: Sketch
bands.payoff: A draft you can use tomorrow

planets.name: The Lead Magnet
planets.chapter: Chapter 2, Leads alone are not enough
planets.blurb: Everything orbits this: one free thing that solves one narrow problem for the people you want, so they raise a hand.

planets.name: Warm Outreach
planets.blurb: Reach out, one at a time, to people who already know you. The cheapest way to your first customers.

planets.name: Free Content
planets.blurb: Post things worth keeping, so strangers become people who know you, and some of them ask.

planets.name: Cold Outreach
planets.blurb: Reach out, one at a time, to people who have never heard of you. Volume, personal first lines, and something of value up front.

planets.name: Paid Ads
planets.blurb: Pay to put your lead magnet in front of strangers. Fast, and it costs money while you learn.
planets.dimMessage: Paid ads spend money while you learn. Say in Start Here that you have a monthly ad budget and this planet lights.

planets.name: Referrals
planets.blurb: Customers who bring customers. The best leads there are, and the only growth that costs nothing.
planets.dimMessage: Referrals need customers to refer. Say in Start Here that you have at least one paying customer and this planet lights.

planets.name: Employees
planets.blurb: People on your team who do the core four for you. Document, demonstrate, duplicate.
planets.dimMessage: This planet is for handing the work to a team. Say in Start Here that you have one, or are hiring, and it lights.

planets.name: Agencies
planets.blurb: Hire an agency to learn a channel from, then bring it in-house.
planets.dimMessage: An agency costs money every month. Say in Start Here that you have a budget and this planet lights.

planets.name: Affiliates
planets.blurb: Other businesses that already serve your customer, sending them to you for a cut.
planets.dimMessage: Affiliates want proof that customers get results. Say in Start Here that you have at least one paying customer and this planet lights.

start.title: Start here
start.chapter: Chapters 1, 3 and 12: the core four, and advertising in real life
start.intro: Six answers. They set which planets light, and they are the promise the book asks you to make: pick one way to get leads, do it a hundred times a day, and keep going until the goal is hit.

fields.label: What you sell, in one line
fields.example: Piano lessons for adults who gave up as kids

fields.label: Who it is for, in one line
fields.example: Busy adults in their 30s and 40s who want to play again

fields.label: Money you could spend on ads each month
options: Some, and I could afford to lose it while I learn

fields.label: Engaged leads you want each week
fields.hint: An engaged lead is someone who gave you a way to reach them and showed interest. The book's whole point is that this is the number to chase.

fields.label: The one core four planet you will start with
options: Free content: I can post every day
Cold outreach: I can do volume
Paid ads: I have money to learn with
fields.hint: The book's order for a one-person business is warm outreach first, then content, then cold, then paid.

start.rule: The rule of 100: a hundred primary actions a day on your first planet. A hundred warm messages. A hundred minutes making content. A hundred cold reach-outs. A hundred dollars of ads. Every day, until the goal is hit.

levels.title: A lead is not an engaged lead
levels.says: A lead is anyone you could contact. An engaged lead is someone who showed interest and gave you a way to reach them. Only engaged leads matter, and a lead magnet is how you make them: one free thing that solves one narrow problem for one kind of person.
levels.checkpoint: You can say who you serve and the one narrow problem the magnet will solve.

fields.label: The person the magnet is for
fields.example: Adults who quit piano as kids

fields.label: The narrow problem it solves, the first step of the bigger one
fields.example: Not knowing which songs are easy enough to start with

levels.title: Pick the kind of magnet
levels.says: There are three kinds. One reveals a problem they did not know they had (a test, a check, an audit). One is a sample or a trial of the real thing. One is a single step of a many-step process, done for them.
levels.checkpoint: One kind chosen, with a reason.

fields.label: The kind
options: One step of a bigger process

fields.label: Why this kind fits the problem
fields.example: They do not know how rusty they are, so a five-minute playing check shows them where to start.

levels.title: How it is delivered
levels.says: A magnet arrives as software, as information, as a service done for them, or as a physical thing. Pick the one they would actually use. Information is easiest to make; a service is hardest to ignore.

fields.label: Delivered as
options: Information: a guide, a video, a list

fields.label: What it is, in one line
fields.example: A twelve-minute video that finds your level and gives you three songs

levels.title: Name it, three ways
levels.says: The name is the headline: what they get, for whom, and why now. Write three, then pick the one a stranger would understand fastest. Test the others later as ad hooks.

fields.label: Name one
fields.example: The Rusty Fingers Test

fields.label: Name two
fields.example: Find your first three songs in twelve minutes

fields.label: Name three
fields.example: The adult beginner's starting map

levels.title: Make it easy to take in
levels.says: The fastest magnet wins. Offer it in the formats people already use, keep it short, and ask for nothing but a way to reach them.
levels.checkpoint: Every box ticked for the magnet as it exists today.
checklist: It takes under fifteen minutes to use
It works on a phone
It comes in the format they prefer (text, video, audio, a tool)
No account or download is needed to get value from it
It asks for one thing only: a way to reach them

levels.title: Make it so good they would pay
levels.says: Give away the thing you could charge for. A magnet that solves the narrow problem completely earns trust for the bigger one. A weak magnet costs you the lead and the reputation.
checklist: It solves the narrow problem completely, not half of it
Someone would pay for it as it stands
It gives a result before they buy anything
It is the best free thing of its kind that you know of
You have used it yourself, start to finish, as a stranger would

levels.title: Tell them what to do next
levels.says: A magnet ends with a call to action: say exactly what to do, and give a reason to do it now. Scarcity, a deadline, or a bonus that goes away all work. A magnet with no ask is a gift, not advertising.
levels.checkpoint: The ask is written and it says why now.

fields.label: The ask, word for word
fields.example: Book a free twenty-minute first lesson this week.

fields.label: The reason to act now
options: None yet, I will add one

levels.title: Count who took it and who engaged
levels.says: Two numbers a month: how many people took the magnet, and how many of those became engaged leads (replied, booked, asked). If the second is a small share of the first, the ask is weak or the magnet drew the wrong people.
levels.checkpoint: Both numbers entered for the last month.

fields.label: People who took the magnet last month

levels.title: More magnets, better magnets, new problems
levels.says: Once one magnet works, make the next: a second narrow problem, a second format, or one magnet per planet. Retire the weakest. The magnet is the start of every planet's funnel, so a better magnet lifts all of them.
checklist: Each planet you use has a magnet that fits how it reaches people
The weakest magnet of the last quarter was retired or rewritten
A second narrow problem has its own magnet
Every magnet ends with the same next step into the paid offer

levels.title: What warm outreach is
levels.says: One-to-one messages to people who already know you: your contacts, your followers, past customers. It costs nothing but time, and it is where the book says a business with no customers starts. The rule of 100 applies: a hundred reach-outs a day.

levels.title: Acknowledge, compliment, ask
levels.says: A warm message is personal or it is spam. Acknowledge something true about them, compliment something real, then ask a question they will want to answer. No pitch in the first message. The pitch comes after they reply.
levels.checkpoint: One real message written for one real person.

fields.label: A real contact (first name is fine)
fields.example: Sam

fields.label: Your acknowledge, compliment, ask
fields.example: Saw you finished the marathon, that is a serious year of training. How are the knees holding up?

levels.title: Get your list
levels.says: Everyone you can reach is your list: phone contacts, email contacts, and followers on every platform. Count them. Most people are surprised how many hundreds they already know.
levels.checkpoint: Every count entered. Zero is fine, blank is not.

levels.title: Pick the platform
levels.says: Reach people where they already answer you. One platform to start. Text if they text you, email if they email you, direct messages if that is where the list lives.

fields.label: Where you will message first
options: Direct messages on a social platform

fields.label: Why there
fields.example: Most of my list is in my phone and they reply to texts within the day

levels.title: Write the offer sentence
levels.says: When someone replies, you tell them what you do in one sentence: I help this kind of person get this result in this much time without this pain. Then the ask: do you know anyone who would want that? Asking about others is easier to say yes to, and often they say me.
levels.checkpoint: All four blanks filled and the sentence reads well out loud.

fields.label: I help
fields.example: adults who quit piano as kids

fields.label: get
fields.example: playing a song they love

fields.label: in
fields.example: thirty days

fields.label: without
fields.example: scales, theory, or a teacher who sighs

reading.template: I help {who} get {outcome} in {time} without {without}. Do you know anyone who would want that?
reading.label: Your offer

levels.title: The daily hundred
levels.says: A hundred personal messages a day, from your list, on your platform. Warm each reply with another acknowledge, compliment, ask before the offer. Log the count. The book's promise is simple: do this every day and the first customers come.
levels.checkpoint: A day where every box is true. Tick it, then log the count on the Machine page.
checklist: The list is open and sorted so you never hunt for the next name
One hundred messages sent, each with a real acknowledge and compliment
Every reply got a second personal message before any offer
The offer sentence was said to everyone who engaged
Everyone who said no was asked if they know someone
Today's count is logged

levels.title: Free, then proof, then a price
levels.says: The first few customers pay with feedback and a testimonial, not money. Serve them so well the results are undeniable. Ask for the testimonial and a referral. Then charge the next batch, and raise the price a little with every batch after that.
checklist: Five people said yes to the free version
Each got more than was promised
Each gave a testimonial in their own words
Each was asked for one referral
The next batch was charged, and the price goes up with each batch

levels.title: Keep the list warm
levels.says: A list goes cold if you only show up to sell. Touch it regularly with something useful or personal, and add every new person you meet to it the same day.
checklist: A monthly note goes to the whole list with something useful, no ask
Every new person you meet is added to the list the same day
Past customers hear from you as often as prospects do

levels.title: Your warm numbers
levels.says: Four numbers a week: messages sent, replies, offers made, and yeses. Reply rate tells you whether the messages are personal. Yes rate tells you whether the offer is good.
levels.checkpoint: All four entered for the last seven days.

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.says: More: a bigger list, from everyone you meet and every customer's circle. Better: a tighter offer sentence and a referral ask every time. New: when warm outreach runs every day without you thinking about it, add the next planet, not before.
checklist: The list grows every week and the growth is counted
The offer sentence was rewritten from what people actually said yes to
Warm outreach runs daily, and someone else could run it from the checklist
The next planet is chosen

levels.title: The content unit: hook, retain, reward
levels.says: Every piece of content does three jobs. The hook earns the first second of attention. The middle keeps it, with a list, steps, or a story. The reward is what they walk away with, so they come back. Post it where the people you want already spend their time.

levels.title: Give, give, give, ask
levels.says: Most content gives and never asks. Some content asks. The ratio is yours to set, and the book's advice is to give far more than you ask. An ask can sit inside a giving piece (integrated) or be its own piece now and then (intermittent).

fields.label: Giving pieces for every asking piece
How you will ask
options: A whole piece, now and then

levels.title: Five hooks from five places
levels.says: Hooks come from topics, and topics come from five places: your far past, your recent past, what is happening now, what is trending, and something you make happen. Write one hook from each. A hook is a headline: a question, a bold claim, a number, or the start of a story.

fields.label: From your far past
fields.example: I quit piano at nine. Here is what I would tell that kid.

fields.label: From your recent past
fields.example: A student played her wedding song last week after six lessons.

fields.label: From right now
fields.example: Teaching the same song to three adults today. Three different mistakes.

fields.label: From a trend
fields.example: That viral piano clip? Here is the one trick that makes it easy.

fields.label: Something you made happen
fields.example: I asked twenty adults why they quit. All twenty said the same thing.

levels.title: Three shapes that keep attention
levels.says: People stay for lists, for steps, and for stories. Outline one piece in each shape from your hooks. Short pieces do one shape; long pieces stack them.

fields.label: A list piece (the hook, then the items)
fields.example: Five songs adults can play in week one: 1. ... 2. ...

fields.label: A steps piece (the hook, then the order)
fields.example: How to relearn a song in a week: day one ... day two ...

fields.label: A story piece (the hook, the turn, the lesson)
fields.example: She had not touched a piano in twenty years. Then ...

levels.title: The reward, and the platform
levels.says: The reward is the reason they follow: they got something they can use. Say what each piece leaves them with. Then pick one platform, the one where your people already are, and stay there until it works.
levels.checkpoint: A platform picked and the reward written.

fields.label: The one platform to start
fields.example: Instagram

fields.label: What a viewer leaves with
fields.example: One thing to try at the piano tonight

levels.title: A week of posting
levels.says: Plan seven pieces, post one a day, and answer everyone who comments. Content compounds: the first week feels like talking to a room with nobody in it. The book says post anyway.
levels.checkpoint: A week where every box is true.
checklist: Seven pieces planned, each with a hook from the five places
Each piece has one shape: list, steps, or story
Each piece names what the viewer leaves with
The give-to-ask ratio was kept
One piece was posted every day
Every comment got a reply

levels.title: A hundred minutes a day
levels.says: The rule of 100 for content is time: a hundred minutes a day making and posting. Log it. Days you skip are days the room stays empty.
levels.checkpoint: A day with the minutes logged.
checklist: A hundred minutes on content today, timed
At least one piece posted
Today's minutes are logged

levels.title: Your content numbers
levels.says: Three numbers a month: pieces posted, followers gained, and engaged leads that came from content. Pieces tell you if you are doing the work. Followers tell you if the hooks work. Engaged leads tell you if the asks work.
levels.checkpoint: All three entered for the last month.

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.says: More: post more often. Better: look at the ten best pieces and make more like them. New: cut long pieces into short ones, take the winners to a second platform, then hand the cutting to someone else.
checklist: The ten best pieces of the quarter are listed with what their hooks had in common
Posting frequency went up and stayed up
Winners are repurposed to a second platform
Someone else cuts long pieces into short ones

levels.title: What cold outreach is
levels.says: One-to-one messages to strangers who fit your customer. It works on four things: a list of the right people, a first line that proves you looked at them, something of real value in the first message, and volume, because most will not answer. Expect to reach many to get one.

levels.title: Get the list
levels.says: Three ways to get names: a tool that finds them, a list you buy, or a list you build by hand from where your customers gather. Start with the one you can have by tomorrow.
levels.checkpoint: A source picked and a count of names in hand.

fields.label: Where the names come from
options: A list I build by hand

levels.title: The first line, and the gift
levels.says: The first line is about them, and it proves a person wrote it. Then give something of value before you ask anything: the lead magnet, a fix, a result they can see fast. Big, fast value is what makes a stranger answer.

fields.label: A first line for one name on the list
fields.example: Your studio's spring recital video has 2,000 views, and the adult students got the loudest cheers.

fields.label: What you give in that first message
fields.example: A free twelve-minute level check for any adult student who wants to restart.

levels.title: The follow-up plan
levels.says: A stranger who did not answer has not said no. Follow up more times than feels comfortable, in more than one way: message, email, a call, a voice note. Decide the number of touches and the channels before you start, so the plan runs itself.
levels.checkpoint: A number of touches and at least two channels.

levels.title: The daily hundred
levels.says: A hundred new cold reach-outs a day, plus every follow-up that is due. Personal first line, the gift, the ask. Log the count.
levels.checkpoint: A day where every box is true.
checklist: One hundred new reach-outs sent
Each had a first line about them
Each gave the gift before any ask
Every follow-up that was due went out, on the planned channel
Today's count is logged

levels.title: Make the volume run itself
levels.says: Volume is the whole game, and volume needs a system: templates with a personal first line, a tool that sends and tracks, a list refilled every week, and, when it works, someone else doing the sending.
checklist: Templates exist for the first message and every follow-up
A tool sends, tracks and reminds you of follow-ups
The list is refilled every week before it runs out
Someone else can run a day from the checklist

levels.title: Your cold numbers
levels.says: Three numbers a week: reach-outs, replies, and bookings. The reply rate tests the first line and the gift. The booking rate tests the ask.
levels.checkpoint: All three entered for the last seven days.

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.says: More: more senders and a bigger list. Better: test first lines and gifts against each other and keep the winner. New: a new list source or a new channel once the current one is steady.
checklist: Two first lines were tested against each other this month and the winner kept
Two gifts were tested the same way
Daily volume went up
A second channel or list source is running

levels.title: What paid ads are, and the money rule
levels.says: You pay a platform to show your lead magnet to strangers. It is the fastest way to reach many, and the only one that costs cash while you learn. Two rules from the book keep it safe: over a customer's life, gross profit should be at least three times what they cost to get, and the first thirty days should bring in twice that cost before you spend more.

levels.title: The parts of an ad
levels.says: Call out the person so the right people stop and the wrong ones scroll on. Hook them the way content does. Give them the value: what they get, for whom, and why now. Then the call to action: the magnet, and one clear step.

levels.title: The platform and the call-out
levels.says: Advertise where your people already are. Then write the labels that call them out: who should see this, and who should not. A good call-out makes a stranger feel found.

fields.label: The platform
fields.example: Facebook and Instagram

fields.label: Who this is for (the labels)
fields.example: Adults over 35 who used to play piano

fields.label: Who should scroll past
fields.example: Parents looking for kids' lessons

levels.title: Write the ad
levels.says: Four pieces, in order. Write it plain. The magnet is the offer in the ad; the paid product comes later.

fields.label: The hook
fields.example: Quit piano as a kid? Your hands remember more than you think.

fields.label: The value: what, for whom, why now
fields.example: A free twelve-minute level check that finds three songs you can play this month. For adults who stopped. Ten spots this week.

fields.label: The call to action
fields.example: Tap to get your level check.

fields.label: The magnet it points to
fields.example: The Rusty Fingers Test

levels.title: Launch day
levels.says: A hundred dollars a day is the book's rule of 100 for ads: enough to learn, small enough to lose. Launch a few versions, capture the contact, and make sure you can see what each lead cost from day one.
levels.checkpoint: Every box ticked on launch day.
checklist: The daily budget is set and you can afford to lose it while you learn
At least three versions of the ad are live (different hooks)
The ad points to the magnet, and the magnet asks for a way to reach them
Cost per lead is visible in the dashboard
A person or a system follows up with every lead the same day

levels.title: The testing loop
levels.says: Every week: keep the winner, kill the losers, launch new challengers. Change one thing at a time, the hook most often. The loop never stops; that is the job.
levels.checkpoint: Every box ticked for the last week.
checklist: The losing versions were turned off
New challengers went live against the winner
One thing changed per challenger
Cost per engaged lead was compared, not just cost per lead

levels.title: Cost per lead, cost per engaged lead, cost per customer
levels.says: Three costs, and they belong on the Machine page where the whole funnel lives: what you spent, how many engaged leads it made, and how many customers. The Machine turns them into the cost of one engaged lead and the cost of one customer.
levels.checkpoint: The Machine has your monthly spend, your funnel rates, and your working days.

levels.title: The three-to-one check
levels.says: Lifetime gross profit divided by the cost of a customer. Under three, fix the offer or the funnel before spending more. The thirty-day check sits beside it: gross profit in the first month against twice the cost of a customer.
levels.checkpoint: The Machine has the price, the margin, and how long a customer stays.

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.says: More: raise the budget while the three-to-one and thirty-day checks hold, and stop the moment they do not. Better: better hooks, tighter call-outs, a stronger magnet. New: a second platform, once the first is boring.
checklist: The budget only rises when both money checks pass
There is a rule for when it falls back
The best hook of the quarter is known and reused
A second platform is being tested with its own small budget

levels.title: Why referrals beat everything
levels.says: A referred customer costs nothing to get, buys more, and stays longer. A business grows on its own only when the customers coming in from referrals outnumber the customers leaving. Referrals come from goodwill, and goodwill is the gap between what you promised and what they got.

levels.title: Make it worth referring
levels.says: Before asking, make the product more referable. The book lists the ways: sell to better-fit customers, set better expectations, get more of them to a result, get them there faster, and keep them longer. Pick the one you will do this quarter.
levels.checkpoint: One picked and the change written.

fields.label: This quarter
options: Get more customers to a result

fields.label: The change, in one line
fields.example: Every new student plays a full song in lesson one, so the first week has a win.

levels.title: How you will ask
levels.says: Six ways to ask, from the book: a reward for the referrer, a reward for both, asking right after a win, bonuses that unlock when they refer, referral events, and a standing program. Choose the ones you will run and write the offer.
levels.checkpoint: At least one way chosen and the offer written.

fields.label: The referral offer, word for word
fields.example: Bring a friend to their first lesson and you both get the next one free.

levels.title: Ask every time
levels.says: The ask lives at two moments: when they buy, and when they win. Make both automatic, track who sent whom, and thank the referrer within the day.
checklist: Every new customer hears the referral offer at signup
Every first win is followed by the ask
Who referred whom is written down
Every referrer is thanked the same day
The referral offer is somewhere customers can find it without asking

levels.title: Referrals in, customers out
levels.says: Two rates a month, and the Machine draws what they do over a year: the share of customers who brought a new one, and the share who left. When the first is bigger than the second, the business grows without ads.
levels.checkpoint: The Machine has your customer count, your referral rate and your churn.

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.says: More: ask at more moments. Better: a bigger reward for the referrer whose people stay. New: the customers who refer most are your first affiliates.
checklist: The referral rate is higher than it was last quarter
The best referrers are named
The best referrers were offered the affiliate deal

levels.title: Someone else does the core four
levels.says: An employee who does one of the core four for you is a lead getter. Training is three steps: document what you do, demonstrate it while they watch, then duplicate: they do it while you watch, until their numbers match yours.

levels.title: Document one job
levels.says: Pick the core four action you do every day and write it as a checklist a stranger could follow. The daily hundred on that planet is the checklist; add the words you say and the numbers you expect.
levels.checkpoint: A job picked and its checklist written.

fields.label: The job to hand off first
The checklist, step by step
fields.example: 1. Open the list. 2. Send 100 messages using the template, first line personal. 3. ...

levels.title: Demonstrate, then duplicate
levels.says: They watch you do a full day. Then you watch them do a full day. Then they do it alone and you check the numbers. Pay for outcomes you can count.
checklist: They watched a whole day of the job, with the checklist in hand
You watched them do a whole day
They did a week alone and the numbers were checked daily
Their pay is tied to a number they control

levels.title: Their numbers against yours
levels.says: One comparison a week: their daily actions and results beside yours from the same job. Train until the gap closes.

fields.label: Your actions a day, same job

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.says: More: a second person on the same job. Better: the best of them trains the next. New: a person on the next planet, and eventually someone who runs the people.
checklist: Two people run the first job
The best of them trains new hires from the checklist
A second planet has its own person
Someone other than you checks the daily numbers

levels.title: Rent the skill, then own it
levels.says: An agency is a way to learn a channel from people who already know it. The book's play: hire one that is good, say up front you plan to bring the work in-house, have your person sit in on everything, then hire a cheaper one to sustain while your person takes over.

levels.title: The interview
levels.says: Ask every agency the same questions and write the answers down. The channel is theirs to run; the learning is yours to keep.
levels.checkpoint: Every question asked of at least two agencies.
checklist: Who exactly will run my account, and how many others do they run
What does the first ninety days look like, week by week
Can my person sit in on every call and see every setting
Show me results for a business like mine, with the numbers
I told them I intend to bring this in-house and asked how they will help

fields.label: The agency you chose, and why
fields.example: Northside, because their person will train mine on the calls

levels.title: Run the engagement
levels.says: Fixed term, weekly calls with your person in the room, every account in your name, and the numbers in your hands every month. When your person can do it, the expensive agency's job is done.
checklist: The contract has an end date
The ad accounts and the pages belong to you, not the agency
Your person is on every weekly call
You get spend, leads, engaged leads and customers every month
Your person has a date to take over

levels.title: What the agency costs per lead
levels.says: The fee plus the spend, over the engaged leads it made. Compare it with what your own planets cost per engaged lead; that is the number that says when to bring it home.
levels.checkpoint: All three entered for last month.

levels.title: Bring it home
levels.says: Your person runs it. A cheaper agency, or none, sustains it. The learning stays.
checklist: Your person runs the channel day to day
The expensive agency is done, or on a smaller retainer
Cost per engaged lead held or fell after the handover

levels.title: Other businesses that send you customers
levels.says: An affiliate already sells to the people you want. Recruiting them is a core four campaign of its own: find them, reach out, make them an offer, get them started, and pay them. One good affiliate can outdo a planet.

levels.title: Who your affiliates are
levels.says: Describe the business that already serves your customer and does not compete with you. Then list twenty of them by name.
levels.checkpoint: The profile written and twenty names counted.

fields.label: The ideal affiliate, in one line
fields.example: Piano shops and tuners who meet adults with a piano gathering dust

levels.title: The affiliate offer
levels.says: What do they get: a share of each sale, a fee per lead, or your product to give their customers. What gets them started: the book favours having them use or buy the product first, and launching together. Write it.
levels.checkpoint: Both chosen and the offer written.

fields.label: What gets them started
options: They use or buy it first

fields.label: The offer, word for word
fields.example: Send us an adult who restarts and we pay you a third of their first month, every time.

levels.title: Recruit and launch
levels.says: Reach the twenty the way you reach any lead: warm if you know them, cold if you do not. Get the first ones started with a launch you run together, and give them everything they need to sell without thinking.
checklist: All twenty were contacted, with the offer
The first affiliate used or bought the product
A launch was run together and the results shared
Every affiliate has ready-made messages, links and the magnet
Payouts go out on a fixed day

levels.title: Your affiliate numbers
levels.says: Two numbers a month: affiliates who sent at least one lead, and the engaged leads they sent. The first says whether they are activated; the second says whether it is worth more of your time.

levels.title: More, better, new
levels.says: More: recruit every month. Better: a leaderboard, tiers and prizes for the ones who send the most. New: a person whose whole job is affiliates.
checklist: Recruiting runs monthly, from a list that is refilled
Affiliates can see how they rank
The top tier earns more
Someone owns the affiliate program

words: Someone who showed interest and gave you a way to reach them. The number the whole book is about.
A free thing that solves one narrow problem for the person you want, in exchange for a way to reach them.
The only four ways to get leads: warm outreach, free content, cold outreach, paid ads. Two are to people who know you and two are to strangers; two are one to one and two are one to many.
Someone who does the core four for you: a customer who refers, an employee, an agency, an affiliate.
A hundred primary actions a day on your chosen planet: messages, minutes of content, reach-outs, or dollars.
You do not stop for the day when the hundred is done; you stop when the goal is hit, or the hundred, whichever is later.
The shape of a warm message: something true about them, something you like, a question they want to answer.
The three jobs of a piece of content.
What a cold message gives before it asks anything.
The three ways to scale any planet: do more of it, do it better, add a new place to do it.
What you spent, divided by the engaged leads it made.
What you spent on getting leads, divided by the customers it made.
Everything a customer pays you over their life, minus what it costs you to deliver it.
The book's rule: lifetime gross profit should be at least three times the cost to get a customer.
Gross profit in a customer's first thirty days should cover the cost to get them twice, so the customers pay for the ads.
The share of customers who leave in a month.
The share of customers who bring a new customer in a month.
How you train someone to do a job: write it down, show them, watch them.
